title: Developing a Departmental Approach to the Do Now
author: Craig Barton
summary: In the first post of his departmental-support series, Craig Barton explains why a Do Now is where he usually starts with a maths department: get it right and both student effort and teacher checking carry into the rest of the lesson. He lists seven ingredients of an effective Do Now, including a clear purpose, a standard format, an easy first question, no more than five questions, and whole-class checks with a rechecked response. A school example shows how the Head of Department's intended routine had drifted into inconsistency because it was mentioned once at the start of term. The agreed routine has five minutes of silent work and then board checks one question at a time, with different responses for nearly-all, some or few correct. The theme is that consistency across a department needs explicit direction, a trial period and rehearsal.
points: A strong Do Now sets the pattern for the rest of the lesson: students start working straight away and the teacher begins with a reliable whole-class check.
Seven ingredients define it, among them a standardised format, an accessible first question, at most five questions, and a check where the teacher sees every student's answer.
The school's inconsistency arose because the intended routine was discussed once in a busy start-of-term meeting and never revisited.
The teacher's response depends on the board evidence (90%+ correct, mixed, under 20%), and a same-difficulty follow-up question is the only proof an explanation worked.
The department trialled the routine with one class for one week, after planning and rehearsing the first lesson together.
quotes: I am a great believer that if you get the Do Now right, it can set up the rest of the lesson. If students crack straight on with work the moment they enter the room, they are more likely to carry this effort through into the rest of the lesson.
Of course, the converse is also true. A sloppy Do Now means both teachers and students are playing catch-up for the rest of the lesson to try to get focus and learning back on track.

This was a surprise to the Head of Department. He had a certain way he wanted the Do Now to be delivered, which he assumed all his colleagues were following. When we dug a little deeper, it turned out that this was discussed briefly in a meeting at the start of term - when colleagues’ heads are full of a million other things - and not revisited again.

Students love copying questions down as it allows them to take a cognitive break whilst busy tricking. As students rarely, if ever, use their exercise books for revising, there is little point in them copying down the questions of the Do Now.

The Do Now should help provide a calm, focused start to the lesson, and should be an opportunity for students to see what they can remember on their own, not what they can remember using cues and hints from their partner. We also wanted to ensure the Do Now did not dominate the lesson, so 5 minutes felt a good time to aim for, with colleagues circulating the room during this time to better judge whether more or less time was needed.

But this can easily be solved by asking students to copy their final answer, without the working, to the first question on their boards ready to show the teacher when instructed. Now, the teacher can see every response, nice and clearly, so immediately knows where understanding is at.

This needs to be quick, 20 seconds maximum, otherwise we may pay the opportunity cost of digging deeper and find ourselves running out of time when understanding is not so secure. Asking a student who got the question wrong to repeat part of our explanation is a better way of assessing whether their understanding is moving in the right direction than the classic: Does that make sense?
